title: The particular judgment (CCC 1021–1022)
hook: at death each person meets Christ

segments.voice: Yesterday, the forgiveness of sins: given in baptism, offered again in confession. Your line was no sin too big. Did an old regret come up, and did the line change anything? Day one thousand eighty-three.

Three crosses on a hill outside Jerusalem. On one side of Jesus, a criminal mocks him. On the other side, a second criminal tells the first to stop: we deserve this, he says, but this man has done nothing wrong. Then he turns his head and asks one thing: remember me when you come into your kingdom. He has no time left to fix anything. No time to make amends, no time to prove he's changed. And the answer he gets doesn't mention later, or someday. It says today. That one word is where the Catechism starts when it talks about what happens at the moment of death.

Here's the answer, in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Amen I say to thee, this day thou shalt be with me in paradise." This day. The Catechism points to that line, and to Jesus's story of the rich man and Lazarus, to teach something Catholics call the particular judgment. Particular, because it's personal: one person, one life, at the moment it ends. First, the meeting. The Letter to the Hebrews says it plainly: "it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment." The Catechism teaches that each person, at death, meets Christ, and their whole life is seen in his light. Second, what happens next. The Catechism names three ways a soul may go: into heaven at once, or into heaven through a purification first, which Catholics call purgatory, or, for someone who has finally refused God's love, lasting separation from him. It doesn't say who goes where. That isn't handed to anyone else to decide. Third, the measure. The Catechism borrows a line from Saint John of the Cross: in the evening of life, he wrote, we will be judged on love. Not on titles, not on how impressive a life looked. On love. And fourth, the hope. Saint Paul wrote that now we see only dimly, as in a dark mirror, "but then face to face." For Catholics, that's the heart of this teaching. Judgment isn't a file read out by a stranger. It's meeting someone, and seeing yourself the way he sees you. The thief on the cross had no record to show. He had one honest request, and a face turned toward Christ.
screen: `THIS DAY THOU SHALT BE WITH ME.` · `ONCE TO DIE, AND AFTER THIS.` · `JUDGED ON LOVE.` · `THEN FACE TO FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: examine today in his light. Some Catholics end the day with a short look back, called an examen, and this is a small version of it. Settle, and breathe. Walk back through today, from waking up until now, slowly, like watching a film. Where was there love: given, received, or missed? Don't argue with yourself or defend anything. Just see it clearly. If you pray, you can imagine looking at the day alongside Christ. If you don't, look at it the way the kindest person you know would look at it. The bell holds the time.
The particular judgment. Catholics believe that at death each person meets Christ, and their life is seen in his light, judged, as John of the Cross put it, on love. Today's word.
Your line: face to face. Today, at one moment, ask what this would look like if it were seen in full, and with love. Then do it that way. Day one thousand eighty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for a holy death and for the dead, and some end the day with an examination of conscience, looking back over the day before God.

notes: CCC paraphrased throughout (1021 refers to the good thief and to Lazarus and the rich man; 1022 the three outcomes and John of the Cross's saying on love). Confirm.
John of the Cross's line is paraphrased ('in the evening of life we will be judged on love'), since the CCC's English is copyrighted. Confirm the wording and the 'Spanish mystic' description.
Confirm Challoner wording of Luke 23:43, Hebrews 9:27 and 1 Corinthians 13:12 ('We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face').
Hell is described as 'separation from him' for 'someone who has finally refused God's love'; confirm tone and accuracy against CCC 1033 and 1022.
Editor pass: cut the unsourced 'Spanish mystic' description of John of the Cross (claims rule); hell now 'lasting separation', closer to CCC 1022's 'everlasting'.
